success_patterns: Distinctive clue details (113-mile, Gulf Coast, 1951, St. James Theatre, Burbank 1972) were matched against passage titles and snippets that repeat them, and the entity recurring across many passages (Padre Island, The King and I, Halloween) was chosen. Several passages were near-verbatim archive hits (J! Archive, Topix, flashcards).

Dictionary-style definition clues ('industrial unit equal to the work one person can do in 60 minutes') were solved by finding a glossary passage ('Man-hours - definition ... An industrial unit of production equal to the work one person can produce...') and answering with its headword in bare singular form.

A 'Category:clue ___' fill-in-the-blank ('Dealing with railroads & aviation:House Committee on ___ & Infrastructure') was answered with only the missing word ('Transportation'), confirmed by the official name that the passages repeat.

A bare quoted slogan ('Tippecanoe and Tyler too') was answered with the principal person it belongs to (William Henry Harrison), not a word from the slogan, not the running mate, and not a description of the slogan.

A leading staging parenthetical ('(Jimmy of the Clue Crew at the St. James Theatre...)') was treated as video-clue decoration. The agent answered from the factual core, 'this musical ... premiered here in 1951', rather than answering with the theatre named in the parenthetical.
Answers stayed bare and short, with no descriptors, and a slot noun such as 'one of these' was filled with the missing member of the set ('subject').

patch.reasoning: These successes show four clue-visible mechanisms that the skill only covers implicitly: Clue Crew staging parentheticals, bare quoted slogans, dictionary-definition clues, and 'Category:... ___' blanks. Writing them down makes the correct reading repeatable. Each edit is short, keyed to a visible clue feature, and placed in the editable rules outside the protected block. None add a mandatory template (earlier template edits regressed) and none conflict with the Rule 3 verbatim override.

edits.target: answer with the common English name (Conch).
edits.content: - A leading parenthetical that only sets the scene for a video clue ('(Jimmy of the Clue Crew at the St. James Theatre in New York City) This musical ... premiered here in 1951', '(Sarah of the Clue Crew ...)') is staging, not a caption for the answer. The place or person in it is an anchor. Answer the 'this <noun>' in the main sentence ('here' = that place), using the remaining details (year, role) to pick the entity. Do not answer with the venue named in the parenthetical.

edits.target: Give the bare name ('Ronald Reagan'), not the event, the place or the date.
edits.content: - A bare quoted slogan, lyric, motto or catchphrase with no blank ('"Tippecanoe and Tyler too"') asks for the principal person, work or organization it belongs to. A campaign slogan -> the candidate at the head of the ticket ('William Henry Harrison', not the running mate or a word from the slogan). Find the passages that tie the phrase to one entity and give that entity's bare name. This is different from a clue with '...' or '___', which asks for the missing word.

edits.target: Answer with only that missing word. If a bare number appears in parentheses, treat it only as this hint, not as part of the question.
edits.content: - Blank-in-a-name clues ('Dealing with railroads & aviation:House Committee on ___ & Infrastructure'): the text before the colon is only a hint. Find the full official name in the passages ('Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure'). Answer with only the words that fill the '___' ('Transportation'), not the whole name.

edits.target: ## Rule 3: Look for the clue repeated verbatim in the context
edits.content: - DEFINITION-STYLE clues ('This industrial unit is equal to the work one person can do in 60 minutes', 'term for ...') are dictionary glosses. Scan the passages for a dictionary, glossary or 'definition of X' page whose gloss paraphrases the clue ('An industrial unit of production equal to the work one person can produce in...'). The answer is that entry's HEADWORD (the page title or the bolded term). Give it in singular, bare form ('Man-hour', not 'Man-hours'), and keep a hyphen if the headword has one.
